A Hong Kong-based company needed two senior React engineers before peak season. Hiring locally meant 60–90 days and $150K+ a year per engineer.

They run a digital marketplace that connects shipping companies with logistics operators. Their checkout was outdated, and conversion was stalling while competitors launched sleeker platforms.

We screened for more than React:
- Next.js depth, tested with a coding challenge.
- A UX case study: walk us through a feature you shipped, what it did for users, and how you measured it.
- A/B testing and conversion experience.
- How clearly each candidate explains technical decisions.

Result: three candidates shortlisted in nine days, two offers accepted, and both engineers productive within 30 days.

In the first 90 days, checkout conversion rose from 4.2% to 4.96%, and A/B testing went from 2 tests a quarter to 4–5 a month.

One detail I like: Hong Kong is only an hour ahead of Jakarta, and the engineers still worked async-first, writing updates and recording decisions. A close time zone doesn't make writing things down optional.

They were hired through our Employer of Record, so the client needed no Indonesian entity.

posts.text:
In Indonesia, shopping spikes follow content, not just calendars. The Ministry of Trade reported that during Harbolnas 2025, 54% of consumers shopped through creator affiliate links and 80% used livestream features.

On Tokopedia and TikTok Shop’s 10.10 promo this year, transactions rose 9x and 4x respectively, according to the platforms.

For anyone running an online store, that changes how you plan for peak days:

• A spike can start in seconds, when a creator goes live or a flash sale opens, not on a schedule

• It doesn’t peak once. It peaks in waves, all day

• The checkout page takes the hit, not the product page

Three things that help:

1. Scale on demand, not on a timetable: auto-scaling that reacts in minutes, and is tested before the day
2. Protect checkout: queues and rate limits, so a wave slows people down instead of breaking things
3. Cache what you can: product pages, images and search results, ahead of the spike

If a creator sold out 10,000 units in ten minutes, what would happen to your checkout?
